author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This code tries to solve the **Predict the Winner** game by recursively exploring picks from either end of `nums` (`left` or `right`), using a `factor` that flips sign on every call to add or subtract the chosen number from a running `sum`, meant to represent the two players alternately maximizing their own advantage; the branches are combined with `&&` when `factor` is positive and `||` when negative, and the base case returns whether the final `sum` is non-negative — but this combinator logic is backwards for a player choosing their *best* move (which only needs one good branch, not both), which is why this attempt is marked as **FAILED**.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This code solves the **Predict the Winner** game with recursive backtracking over two pointers, `left` and `right`, using a `factor` (starting at `-1` and flipping sign each call) to alternately add or subtract the picked number (`nums[left]` or `nums[right]`) from a running `sum`, which tracks the score difference between the two optimally-playing players; when `factor` is positive it takes the `||` of the two choices since the current player only needs one favorable path to win, and when negative it takes the `&&` since the opponent is assumed to always respond optimally, with the function ultimately returning whether the final `sum` is non-negative (meaning the first player wins or ties).

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is the same alternating min/max recursion as the previous solution, but adds **memoization** via a `Map` keyed on the stringified `[left, right, factor, sum]` tuple, so before doing any work `dfs` checks whether that exact state has already been solved and returns the cached boolean instead of recomputing it, storing each new result in the map before returning — trading extra memory for avoiding redundant recursive calls.

author: Leetcode
aiExplanation: This solution reframes the problem around the **maximum score difference** the current player can achieve over their opponent: `dfs(left, right)` picks either `nums[left]` or `nums[right]` and subtracts the opponent's best possible outcome on the remaining subarray (`nums[left] - dfs(left + 1, right)` vs. `nums[right] - dfs(left, right - 1)`), taking whichever is larger via `Math.max`; results are memoized in a `Map` keyed by `"left:right"` to avoid recomputing overlapping subproblems, and the first player wins or ties whenever this maximum difference is non-negative.

author: Leetcode
aiExplanation: This solution converts the same score-difference idea into an efficient **bottom-up dynamic programming** approach using a single 1D array `dp`, where `dp[j]` is progressively updated to hold the best achievable score difference for the subarray between the current `i` and `j` via `Math.max(nums[i] - dp[j], nums[j] - dp[j - 1])`, iterating `i` from right to left and `j` from `i + 1` onward so each cell reuses previously computed values in place; it also short-circuits by immediately returning `true` when `nums` has an even length, since the first player is always guaranteed to win in that case, and otherwise returns whether `dp[n - 1]` is non-negative.
